extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians and graduate students working on Ricci flow and geometric analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and records geometric definitions, lemmas, and theorems used to study ancient κ-solutions of the Ricci flow (ε-necks, bump theorems, point-picking lemmas, convergence to shrinking solitons). Focuses on hypotheses and conclusions used for blow-up/limit arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: ε-neck (of radius r)
rubrics_metrics.description: An open subset N is an ε-neck of radius r if (N, r^{-2} g_{ij}) is ε-close, in the C^{[ε^{-1}]} topology, to a standard neck S^{n-1} × I, where S^{n-1} is the round (n-1)-sphere with scalar curvature 1 and I is an interval of length 2ε^{-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a scale-invariant geometric closeness notion: one rescales the metric by r^{-2} and requires C^{k}-closeness (k ≈ ε^{-1}) to the model product metric. Used to identify neck-like regions and to control their radii in noncompact manifolds with nonnegative sectional curvature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 6.1.1 — ε-neck radius lower bound
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists ε0 = ε0(n) such that every complete noncompact n-dimensional Riemannian manifold (M,g) of nonnegative sectional curvature has a positive r0 so that any ε-neck of radius r with ε ≤ ε0 must have r ≥ r0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents arbitrarily small necks (in radius) occurring in such manifolds; used in contradiction/compactness arguments to obtain control over neck scales at infinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: curvature β-bump and λ-remote (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A geodesic ball B(p,r) is a curvature β-bump if the sectional curvature K ≥ β / r^2 at all points in the ball. The ball B(p,r) is λ-remote from an origin O if d(p,O) ≥ λ r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These quantifications measure 'localized high curvature' (β-bump) and how far such bumps sit relative to their radius (λ-remote). They are the basic objects in Hamilton's finite bump statement and in controlling the number and location of curvature concentrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite Bump Theorem (Hamilton)
rubrics_metrics.description: For every β > 0 there exists λ < ∞ such that in any complete manifold of nonnegative sectional curvature there are at most a finite number of disjoint balls which are λ-remote curvature β-bumps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a global finiteness control on disjoint remote curvature concentrations. Used to deduce structure at infinity and to help produce splitting or dimension-reduction limits in blow-up arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 6.1.2 (Chen–Zhu) — splitting of limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose (M,g) is a complete n-dimensional Riemannian manifold with nonnegative sectional curvature. Fix P in M; let P_k be points with d(P,P_k) → ∞ and let λ_k > 0 be scaling factors. If the marked manifolds (M, λ_k^2 g, P_k) converge in C^∞_loc to a limit manifold, then the limit manifold splits isometrically as R × N (a line factor times a lower-dimensional manifold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses include nonnegative sectional curvature and C^∞_loc convergence of pointed rescalings. The conclusion provides a product (line) factor in any noncompact blow-up limit when the basepoints escape to infinity fast enough (λ_k d(P,P_k) → ∞).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 6.1.3 (Hamilton) — point-picking at infinity when Asymptotic Scalar Curvature Ratio = ∞
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a complete noncompact Riemannian manifold with bounded curvature and asymptotic scalar curvature ratio A = lim sup_{s→∞} R s^2 = ∞, one can find points x_j → ∞, radii r_j and numbers δ_j → 0 such that: (i) R(x) ≤ (1+δ_j) R(x_j) for all x in B(x_j, r_j); (ii) r_j^2 R(x_j) → ∞; (iii) λ_j := d(x_j,O)/r_j → ∞; (iv) the balls B(x_j, r_j) are disjoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constructs almost-maximal curvature centers at infinity with controlled neighborhoods and separated scales—useful to produce rescaled limits and to ensure blow-up regions are well-controlled and isolated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 6.1.4 — local almost-maximum curvature points for unbounded curvature
rubrics_metrics.description: If a complete noncompact Riemannian manifold has unbounded curvature, there is a sequence of points x_j → ∞ such that |Rm(x_j)| ≥ j and for each j one has |Rm(x)| ≤ 4 |Rm(x_j)| for x in the ball B(x_j, j / sqrt{|Rm(x_j)|}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a simple iterative construction of points where the curvature is large and locally essentially maximal within a radius comparable to j/√(curvature). This yields canonical centers for rescaling in the unbounded-curvature case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — ancient κ-solution
rubrics_metrics.description: A solution to the Ricci flow is called an ancient κ-solution if it is complete (compact or noncompact), defined on an ancient time interval (−∞, T) with T > 0, has nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature, and is κ-noncollapsed on all scales for some κ > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancient κ-solutions are the canonical blow-up limits arising from finite-time singularities in 3D Ricci flow; the definition packages curvature nonnegativity, boundedness, and noncollapsing needed for compactness theorems and classification results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Li–Yau–Perelman distance inequalities and gradient bound
rubrics_metrics.description: The Li–Yau–Perelman reduced distance l(q,τ) satisfies differential inequalities (6.2.2)–(6.2.4) (relations for ∂l/∂τ, ∆l, |∇l|^2 terms) and in particular the estimate |∇l|^2 + R ≤ 3 l / τ holds for ancient κ-solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These inequalities control the behavior of reduced distance and scalar curvature along minimizing L-geodesics; they are essential inputs to monotonicity of reduced volume and to deriving a priori bounds used in compactness and limit arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perelman's reduced volume monotonicity and upper bound
rubrics_metrics.description: Perelman's reduced volume ˜V(τ) satisfies monotonicity (nonincreasing in τ) and the Jacobian comparison gives ˜V(τ) ≤ 1; for a nonflat ancient κ-solution one has ˜V(τ) < 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monotonicity and the strict inequality for nonflat solutions are used to rule out flat limits and to deduce that any nonflat blow-up limit (constructed via reduced volume limits) must have reduced volume strictly less than 1, which helps identify nonflat shrinking solitons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 6.2.1 (Perelman) — asymptotic shrinking soliton
rubrics_metrics.description: Let g_{ij}(·,t), t ∈ (−∞,T) (T>0), be a nonflat ancient κ-solution. Then there exist points q_k and times t_k → −∞ such that the rescalings of g_{ij} around q_k with factor |t_k|^{-1} (and time shifted so t_k → 0) converge in C^∞_loc to a nonflat gradient shrinking soliton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the main asymptotic statement: every nonflat ancient κ-solution has at least one nonflat shrinking soliton as a pointed limit under appropriate backward rescalings. The proof uses reduced distance bounds, reduced volume monotonicity, point-picking and compactness theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradient shrinking soliton characterization equation
rubrics_metrics.description: A limit gradient shrinking soliton arising in the scaling limit satisfies the soliton equation Ric_{ij} + ∇_i ∇_j f − (1/2s) g_{ij} = 0 (with the Perelman potential f = l and parabolic parameter s); equivalently identities derived from the reduced-volume Euler–Lagrange equations hold (see (6.2.23)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This PDE characterization identifies the limit as a gradient shrinking soliton. In the limit one also obtains vanishing of certain integrands (e.g. squared norms) showing the soliton equations hold; these identities are used to classify the limit geometry.
